```{r}
cohort <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("outputs", "tables", "recruitment-cohort-flow.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  dplyr::filter(.data$cohort == "Reconciled recruitment cohort")
counts <- readr::read_csv(
  here::here("outputs", "tables", "recruitment-model-count-strata.csv"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
high <- dplyr::filter(counts, .data$count_group == ">20")
stopifnot(nrow(cohort) == 1, nrow(high) == 1)
```

These figures show where the study observations come from, how starting
seedling counts relate to recorded sapling entry, and whether additional
maple measurements improve prediction. The [research paper](recruitment.qmd)
provides the methods, full results, and limitations.

## Where the observations come from

I analyzed `r scales::comma(cohort$conditions)` pairs of forest-condition
observations on `r scales::comma(cohort$physical_plots)` physical plots across
`r cohort$counties` Michigan counties. Each pair links a sampled forest area
across two visits.

The map shows the number of retained observation pairs in each county.
Brighter yellow marks larger counts; gray marks counties with no retained
pairs. The legend labels the counts, with a square-root color scale to make
variation visible. The map describes the geographic coverage of the sample.
It does not estimate a county's recruitment rate or regeneration quality.

```{r}
#| label: fig-recruitment-map
#| fig-cap: "Recruitment observations by county. Fill represents the number of retained forest-condition pairs, with a square-root color scale. County identifiers provide the spatial link; the analysis does not use or infer exact FIA plot locations."
#| fig-alt: "Michigan counties shaded from dark purple for smaller sample counts to yellow for larger counts. Northern counties contain most retained pairs; counties without retained pairs are gray."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("outputs", "figures", "07_recruitment_cohort_map.png"))
```

## What starting seedling counts tell us

Conditions with more recorded seedlings at baseline more often contained a
new live maple sapling at the next visit. Among the
`r high$conditions` conditions with more than 20 starting seedlings,
`r high$conditions_with_new_tally`
(`r scales::percent(high$recruitment_fraction, accuracy = 0.1)`)
had a qualifying new sapling. The remaining conditions had no qualifying
recorded entry on the sampled area.

```{r}
#| label: fig-seedling-entry
#| fig-cap: "Recorded sapling entry by starting maple seedling count. Bar labels show conditions with entry divided by all conditions in each group. Vertical lines show uncertainty from resampling whole counties. A group with no observed events has a zero-width empirical interval; it does not establish zero population probability."
#| fig-alt: "Recorded entry increases from 0 of 250 conditions with no starting seedlings to 72 of 280 conditions with more than 20 seedlings, or 25.7 percent."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("outputs", "figures", "10_recruitment_counts.png"))
```

A qualifying sapling has a trunk at least 1 inch but less than 5 inches in
diameter at breast height. The inventory does not individually link each
baseline seedling to a later sapling. These observations therefore show
recorded entry without establishing adequate replacement of canopy trees.

## Do additional maple measurements improve prediction?

I compared models on identical observations and tested them on counties
excluded from training. The first comparison adds seedling count to sampling
coverage and elapsed time. The second adds existing maple sapling density
and established-maple basal area to that count model.

The horizontal axis shows the change in average probability error, measured
by the Brier score. Values to the left of zero favor the added measurements.
The horizontal lines show 95% intervals from resampling counties and
refitting the models. An interval crossing zero includes both improvement
and worsening.

```{r}
#| label: fig-added-maple-information
#| fig-cap: "Change in Brier score when measurements are added to the model. Negative differences indicate lower probability error. The two panels evaluate all eligible observations and the subset with starting seedlings. The subsets overlap and do not provide independent replications."
#| fig-alt: "Adding seedling count improves Brier score across all eligible observations. Intervals cross zero for the additional maple size measurements in both populations and for seedling count within the baseline-detected subset."
#| out-width: "100%"
knitr::include_graphics(here::here("outputs", "figures", "11_recruitment_incremental_value.png"))
```

Counts improved average probability error across all eligible observations.
Within the subset that already contained seedlings, the Brier improvement
was less certain. Adding maple size measurements produced small point
improvements, with intervals crossing zero in both populations. These
comparisons did not establish a dependable predictive advantage from the
additional size measurements.

The [full results](recruitment.qmd#results) also report calibration, other
performance measures, sensitivity checks, and the fates of tagged saplings.
